item.text: {"verdicts":[{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E001","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E002","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"IMSS-BIENESTAR’s rules described preventive, epidemiological, ambulatory, hospital, specialty, palliative and rehabilitation services, associated medicines, community participation and citizen oversight for people without social security. They listed 4,075 national units and hospitals, based on a September 2022 catalogue, described itinerant services for geographically dispersed populations, and stated that federalization would expand coverage and contribute to universal and free access. The population registry could include migrants receiving program services.","notes":["The excerpt lists 4,075, not merely a count of hospitals and health units independently verified in 2023.","The text describes intended or authorized arrangements and a proposed federalization strategy, not completed expansion or effective universal coverage."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E003","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E004","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"The rules prescribed multidisciplinary supervision and advisory visits, written commitments, performance and quality reviews, corrective measures, internal and external evaluations, and public reporting of external evaluation results. The program unit was authorized to administer operating resources, coordinate training strategies, and approve or sanction actions concerning procurement, infrastructure, equipment and improvement.","notes":["The excerpt supports formal authority and mechanisms, but not independent evaluations or demonstrated effectiveness."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E005","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"The rules linked budget preparation to national and sectoral plans and results indicators, assigned resources to OOADs according to coverage and activity, required separate and detailed accounting, required unspent Ramo 19 funds to be returned to the Treasury, subjected expenditures to federal review and audits, and required internal follow-up and reports on audit recommendations. Internal monitoring used a semaforized control dashboard, and external evaluations were assigned to recognized specialists or institutions with public reporting of results.","notes":["The excerpt does not state that all expenditures were actually audited; it says they could be reviewed by specified authorities.","The rules prescribe controls and evaluations, not their completed operation or findings."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E006","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E007","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"Amnesty International reported that Mexico supported recommendations concerning investigation and sanction of security-force abuses, journalist protection, strengthening the National Human Rights Commission and arraigo. It stated that impunity remained a major challenge, journalist investigations remained inadequate, arraigo provisions remained in force, and the recommendation to strengthen NHRC autonomy and capacities had not yet been implemented.","notes":["The excerpt attributes these findings to Amnesty International and its cited assessment; it does not establish that all failures were personally attributable to López Obrador."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E008","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"The report stated that the president publicly attacked the Supreme Court after it blocked his attempt to place the National Guard under military control, and that he accused Indigenous and environmental defenders concerned about the Mayan Train of being “false environmentalists.” It also reported stigmatization, repression, disproportionate or unnecessary force, arbitrary arrests, sexual violence, criminalization of protest and impunity in the situations discussed.","notes":["The excerpt does not support the added period-specific claim about an April 2023 ruling; that appears elsewhere in the supplied material, not the quoted excerpt.","The abuses are not all attributed personally to the president."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E009","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E010","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E011","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"CIDOB identifies López Obrador as Mexico’s president from 2018 to 2024 and describes the 2018–2024 platform as emphasizing austerity, social programs addressing poverty and violence, energy and food self-sufficiency, anti-corruption, gradual withdrawal of the armed forces from internal security, and cooperation with the United States. It also describes a pragmatic social-democratic platform combining macroeconomic stability and budget discipline with rejection of privatization and foreign control in strategic sectors.","notes":["The excerpt supports the programmatic baseline, not implementation or 2023 outcomes.","The specific phrase “reducing poverty and violence” is narrowed to the platform’s stated aims."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E012","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"López Obrador’s 2018 program, as described by CIDOB, included legality and anti-corruption, poverty reduction, peace, austerity, gender equity, sustainable development and reconstruction. It proposed withdrawing the armed forces from internal-security missions while organizing and deploying a National Guard to pacify Mexico. His coalition later obtained an absolute majority in both federal chambers.","notes":["The excerpt does not specify civilian command for the National Guard; it describes a new armed body intended to replace or reduce the Army’s internal-security role.","The excerpt supports coalition majorities, not a broader claim of extensive subnational representation."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E013","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"CSIS assessed López Obrador’s policies as producing mixed results and, in some areas, counterproductive effects. It described increased military influence despite demilitarization rhetoric, centralization of power and weakening of independent checks, an insufficient nearshoring strategy, deteriorating security, personal austerity and persistent anti-corruption rhetoric. It also credited restrained pandemic spending with avoiding a significant fiscal crisis and credited him with successfully negotiating the USMCA.","notes":["The excerpt does not explicitly support the broader claim that security deterioration was caused by the administration, beyond its analytical assessment of policy effects."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E014","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E015","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E016","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E017","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"CSIS reported about 34,000 homicides in 2021, described 2022 as the most violent year recorded by the National Public Security System, reported 100 political assassinations during the 2021 midterm elections, and stated that criminal organizations had expanded control to claim up to 40 percent of Mexican territory. It assessed the “abrazos, no balazos” policy as associated with expanding criminal control, reduced security spending and reduced U.S. security and counternarcotics cooperation.","notes":["The excerpt does not use the exact wording “ineffective”; it presents an adverse analytical assessment and associated trends."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E018","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E019","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E020","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E021","status":"corrected","corrected_fact_summary":"The presentation described Mexico’s recovery as somewhat slow but supported by solid macroeconomic fundamentals, and stated that Mexico had adopted a conservative pandemic fiscal policy, had a low relative primary balance and manageable current-account levels. It also identified incomplete global recovery, high inflation, expected global monetary tightening and uncertainty related to Ukraine as challenges.","notes":["The excerpt does not state that the fiscal policy was López Obrador’s personal decision or directly attribute the macroeconomic conditions to him.","“Relatively low primary balance” is the excerpt’s wording; it does not establish overall fiscal management as successful."]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E022","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E023","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E024","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E025","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E026","status":"accepted","corrected_fact_summary":null,"notes":[]}]}
